events.title: A new bishop
events.body: The announcement comes at six in the morning, Rome time, and by the time you have said the seven o'clock Mass the presbyterate has read it twice and begun to sort itself. {@bishop.full} will be installed in six weeks. The photograph in the diocesan paper shows a man you have never met, in a see you have never visited, smiling the way men smile when they have been told to. Everyone who has been anyone under the last bishop is on the phone by noon, and everyone who was not is being careful not to look pleased. You know, because it is your job to know, what you have said in public and to whom, and you know that all of it will now be read by a stranger. The vicar general sends round a note asking the priests not to speculate. The priests speculate. What you do in the next six weeks will be remembered by a man who does not yet know your name, and by the men who intend to tell him.
events.flavorPrompt: The morning a diocese finds out who it belongs to now.

choices.label: Write him a letter of welcome, brief and unfussy, and say nothing else
choices.outcome: You write four sentences and mean them. It goes in the pile with two hundred others, and his secretary reads it, and it is the kind of letter a secretary remembers. You do not mention the last bishop. The vicar general notices that you did not call.

choices.label: Ask for ten minutes with him in the first month, and use them
choices.outcome: You get eight. He is tired and courteous and wants to know what the parishes actually need, and you tell him, and he writes one thing down. You will never know which. Brother priests hear that you went and draw their own conclusions about why.

choices.label: Do nothing. Let him find you where you are, or not
choices.outcome: You say your Masses and answer no phones about it. It is either the most dignified thing you have done or a decision you will regret in two years, and you will not know which for two years. The men who went to see him will know your name before he does.

choices.label: Preach on obedience to the new shepherd the Sunday after the installation, by name
choices.outcome: The homily is repeated to him within the week, which you knew it would be. If he is the kind of man who wanted that, you have made a friend at the top; if he is not, you have told him exactly what you think a bishop is for. Either way the parish knows where you stand, and so does the diocesan paper.

events.title: The revaluation
events.body: Within a month of the installation you understand the new arithmetic. Men who were exiled to the county's far end under the last bishop are having lunch on the second floor of the chancery. Men who were on every committee have stopped being asked. You are one or the other, and everyone knows which, because you have said things in public for years and the things are written down. A classmate calls to say, kindly, that your name came up. He will not say in what tone. The vicar for clergy, who has survived three bishops by having no opinions, asks whether you would like to talk about your future, which is what he says to men who are about to be moved and to men who are about to be promoted, and he says it in the same voice to both. You could recant nothing and let the record stand. You could find a way to be useful that has nothing to do with what you believe. Or you could write to {@bishop} directly and tell him what you think he has heard, and what you would say to it.
events.flavorPrompt: The moment a man with a public record learns what it is worth under the new bishop.

choices.label: Let the record stand, say nothing, and be what you have been
choices.outcome: Consistency has a price and a value and you have chosen to pay the one for the other. Brother priests on both sides note that you did not trim. Whether the bishop notices depends on whether anyone tells him, and the men who would tell him are not your friends.

choices.label: Make yourself useful in a way that has nothing to do with belief: volunteer for the thing nobody wants
choices.outcome: You take the assignment that has no politics in it, the one with the debt and the boiler, and you do it well, and the new bishop learns your name as a man who fixes things. It is not who you are. It is who you can afford to be for a few years.

choices.label: Write to him directly: here is what you have heard about me, and here is what I would say to it
choices.outcome: Two pages, no adjectives. He answers in three lines, by hand, which is either a kindness or a warning. Men who write to bishops uninvited are either brave or foolish and the bishop decides which; you have made it his decision, at least, rather than the vicar for clergy's.

events.title: The letter at seventy-five
events.body: Canon law requires it and the chancellor's office sends a reminder in case you forgot, which you did not. You are to write to the bishop offering your resignation from your office, and he is to accept it or not, and everyone knows that in this diocese he will not, not this year, because there is no one to replace you. So the letter is a form. You sit down to write the form. What comes out is not a form. You find you have things to say about forty-odd years, about the parishes and the men who ran them and the two or three people who taught you the job, and about what it has cost, and the page fills. You will not send that version. But you have written it now, and it is in the drawer, and it is the truest account of your life that exists.
events.flavorPrompt: An old priest writing the letter that will not be accepted.

choices.label: Send the form. Keep the other page in the drawer
choices.outcome: Three sentences, correct and cold, go to the chancery. The other page stays. Someone will find it after you, and it will explain more than the sacramental registers do.

choices.label: Send the true version
choices.outcome: It is read, which surprises you, and quoted back to you at the next clergy day by a bishop who is not usually sentimental. Men come up afterward. Whether it hastens or delays your going, you have said what you had to say to the institution that had you, and it heard.

events.title: The Sounding-Out
events.body: It happens after lunch on the clergy day, in the corridor by the coat racks, which is where the diocese does its real business. {@vicar_for_clergy} falls into step beside you and asks how the year has been, and you tell him, and then he says that the bishop is beginning to think about June. Nothing is decided. Nothing is even proposed. He wonders, in the voice of a man wondering aloud, what you would say to something out in the county, or something with a school, or something with a second priest in the house. He does not name a parish. He watches you not ask him to. This is the sounding-out, and every priest in {diocese} has had one and most of them did not recognize it at the time. Whatever you say in the next four minutes will be written on a legal pad tonight in a form you would not recognize either, and read aloud in a room you will never enter, by men deciding whether you are the kind of priest who can be sent or the kind who has to be asked.
events.flavorPrompt: A corridor conversation that is an interview. The vicar for clergy is pleasant and gives nothing away.

choices.label: Say you will go where you are sent, and mean it
choices.outcome: He nods as if you had said something ordinary, which in this diocese you have not. The pad that night says available, which is the best word a file can hold and also the most dangerous, because the parish nobody wants is always looking for an available man.

choices.label: Name the two parishes you would want and the one you would not
choices.outcome: He does not write anything down in the corridor, but he repeats the three names back to you, which is worse. You have been honest and specific, and the file will now say so, and in the chancery honest and specific is read as a man with a list. Some bishops like a man with a list. You do not yet know which kind you have.

choices.label: Ask what happened to the last man in whichever parish he means
choices.outcome: There is a pause, and then he tells you, briefly and fairly, because you asked the question a priest asks rather than the one a candidate asks. You learn something about the parish and something about how the diocese talks about men who leave parishes. The pad says shrewd. It is not clear whether that is a compliment.

choices.label: Say you are happy where you are and would rather not be moved
choices.outcome: He says that is good to hear, and it is, and it goes on the pad as settled, which is the word for men the board stops discussing. Your parish will keep you a while longer. The men who said anywhere will be pastors before you, and some of them will be miserable, and you will not be one of them.

events.title: Not This Year
events.body: The June appointments are printed in the diocesan paper on a Thursday, two columns, name and parish and effective date, and you read it the way everyone reads it, from the top, looking for one name. It is not there. Nobody called beforehand, which is itself information. On Friday {@vicar_for_clergy} does call, and the call is kind and short and contains the sentence every priest in {diocese} can recite: the bishop has you very much in mind, and it was a thin year for openings, and not this year. He does not say what the board said. He does not say who else was considered, or for what, or whether your name came up at all, and he has been doing this long enough that you cannot tell from his voice which of those it was. Then he asks about the parish, and you tell him, and the call ends. The 8:00 Mass on Saturday has eleven people in it and one of them has read the paper and does not know whether to say anything.

choices.label: Say the Mass, and say nothing about the list to anyone
choices.outcome: You do the week as if the paper had not come. It is the discipline the life asks for and you find you have it. Whether it is peace or numbness you will know by Advent. The parish, which noticed, decides you are a man who does not sulk, and the parish is not wrong.

choices.label: Go to the chancery and ask him, in his office, what the board actually said
choices.outcome: He closes the door, which he does not do for everyone, and tells you two things: one about the parish that went to someone else and one about you. The second is the useful one and it stings. You leave knowing what the file says, which is more than most men ever learn, and he leaves knowing you will ask again.

choices.label: Say at the deanery lunch what you think of how this diocese makes its lists
choices.outcome: It gets a laugh and two nods and one silence, and the silence belongs to the man who reports the deanery lunch to the second floor. The brother priests like you more for it. The chancery, which never minded that you were passed over, now minds that you said so.

choices.label: Write to {@bishop}: that you would like to be considered, and why
choices.outcome: A page, no more, with three concrete things you have done and one thing you would want to do. He answers in a fortnight, briefly and by hand, thanking you for your candor. Men who write are remembered, sometimes fondly. The vicar for clergy hears about the letter and is not offended, only interested.

events.title: The Second Name
events.body: Everyone knew the parish was opening; the pastor had said so at Easter and been visibly relieved. What you did not know until {@closest_classmate} told you, over the phone, in the voice he uses for things he should not be telling you, is that the personnel board sent the bishop three names for it and yours was one. The other two were {@brother_priest} and a man from the far end of the diocese, and the bishop chose {@brother_priest}, and the letter has gone out, and the installation is on the feast of the parish's patron a month from now. The dean has already asked you to concelebrate, in the tone of a man who does not know and would rather not. {@closest_classmate} says the board's vote was not close and will not say in which direction. You have been measured against two other priests by men who know all three of you, and you came second or third, and there is no appeal, and a month from now you will put on a chasuble and stand at the side of the altar while the man who came first is given the keys.
events.flavorPrompt: Losing a terna; the classmate's phone call; the installation coming.

choices.label: Concelebrate at his installation and mean the handshake
choices.outcome: You stand where the dean puts you and sing what the choir sings and at the sign of peace {@brother_priest} holds your hand a second longer than the rite requires, because he knows. Afterward, at the reception, three priests notice that you came, and one of them is on the board.

choices.label: Ask {@vicar_general} what tipped it
choices.outcome: He tells you, because you have earned the telling, and because he thinks you can bear it. It was one thing, and it was not the thing you feared, and it is fixable in the sense that a man can fix something about himself over four or five years. You thank him. He says not to make a habit of asking.

choices.label: Let {@closest_classmate} tell you what was said in the room
choices.outcome: He tells you more than he should, and you both know it, and it binds you closer and makes him a little afraid of what he has done. You learn how the board talks about you when you are not there. Some of it is fair. You will not be able to un-hear the rest, and he will not be able to un-say it.

choices.label: Decide, privately, that you are not going to be made pastor here, and turn to the work in front of you
choices.outcome: It is not bitterness, or not only. It is a decision to stop reading the June list, and it frees an hour a week you did not know you were spending. The parish gets the hour. Whether the board will notice that you have stopped wanting it, and whether that changes anything, is a question you have decided not to ask.

events.title: How You Got It
events.body: The letter said the bishop had consulted the personnel board and appointed you, and that was all it said, and for a while that is all you knew. Then the deanery meets, and afterward, at the sandwiches, a pastor you barely know tells you in a friendly way that you were the second name on the terna, and that the first name turned it down, or was crossed out, depending on which version he heard. He says it as if it were nothing, and in his experience it is: everyone in {diocese} is somebody's second name. But it means there is a folder at the chancery with three priests in it and a page about each, and the page about you says what three or four men who have watched you for years think you are good for and what they think you are not. You will run {parish} for six years on the strength of that page. You could go on not knowing what it says. Most men do. Most men wonder.
events.flavorPrompt: A new pastor learning, at the sandwiches, that he was the second name.

choices.label: Never ask. It is yours now, however it came
choices.outcome: You decide the folder is the diocese's business and the parish is yours, and it is a relief to have decided it. Years later a chancellor mentions the terna in passing and you find you no longer want to know. That, you think, is what it means to have become the pastor.

choices.label: Find out who the first name was
choices.outcome: It takes two lunches and costs you a little of the reputation for not caring about such things that you had been building. You learn the name and the reason he is not sitting where you are sitting, and the reason is instructive, and you will think about it every time you are tempted the same way.

choices.label: Write to {@vicar_for_clergy} to thank the board, and say what you intend for {parish}
choices.outcome: A page. He reads it to the board at their next meeting, which you did not intend and could not have prevented, and it lands well, because pastors do not usually write to the board except to complain. The page goes in the folder, on top. It is the first thing in it that you wrote yourself.

choices.label: Go and see {@brother_priest}, who was on the list and is not the pastor
choices.outcome: He knows why you have come before you have said it, and he is gracious about it in a way that costs him something visible. You talk about the parish, not the terna. When you leave he says he would have done it differently, and tells you how, and half of it is good advice.

events.title: The Courtesy Call
events.body: {@vicar_for_clergy} calls on a Tuesday evening, which he does not do, and says he is calling as a courtesy, which means the thing is decided. The bishop intends, in June, to send you to a parish you have heard of the way one hears of a distant relative's illness: two hours out, a school that will close within the year whatever anyone does, a rectory nobody has painted since the last pastor left in a hurry for reasons the diocese does not discuss on the telephone. The letter will come next week and will say that the bishop is confident of your generosity. He is telling you now so that you are not surprised, and so that if you are going to say something you say it to him and not to the paper. He is fair about it. He does not pretend it is a promotion, or a punishment, or anything but what it is: a parish that needs a priest and a priest the diocese can spare. You have a week in which nothing is official and everything is settled, and what you do with the week is the only part of this that is yours.
events.flavorPrompt: The call before the letter: a parish no one asked for, delivered kindly.

choices.label: Say yes on the phone, and ask him to send the parish file tonight
choices.outcome: There is a silence on the line that is the sound of a man revising his opinion of you. The file comes by email within the hour: the debt, the roll, the last three pastors' terms. You read it before bed. It is worse than he said and you are, by morning, already thinking about the boiler.

choices.label: Ask him, plainly, whether the bishop would reconsider
choices.outcome: He says he will ask, and he does, and what comes back is a second call, kinder, and no change. You have spent a favor to learn that the letter was already signed when he rang. He does not hold it against you. The bishop, who now knows you asked, will remember the asking longer than the going.

choices.label: Accept, and name what the parish will need from the diocese to survive
choices.outcome: You have the numbers because you looked them up while he was talking. A bookkeeper two days a week, the roof loan restructured, a year's grace on the assessment. He writes them down. Two of the three arrive in the letter. You have gone where you were sent and not gone empty-handed, and the chancery has learned you read balance sheets.

choices.label: Tell {@closest_classmate} what you think of it, and no one else
choices.outcome: You say it once, late, on the phone, all of it, and he lets you. Then he says the thing about the last man there that nobody at the chancery would have told you, and it changes how you think about the parish. Nothing you said leaves the call. Something he said arrives with you in June.

events.title: The Six-Year Letter
events.body: The chancery's letter arrives in Lent and is one paragraph long. Your term as pastor of {parish} concludes at the end of June; the bishop, in accordance with the diocese's policy on the term of office of pastors, invites you to indicate whether you would accept appointment to a second term, and encloses a form. The form has three boxes. Six years ago the parish was a place you were sent. Now it is the parish where you buried the finance chair's wife and baptized her grandchildren and know which door of the sacristy sticks in August, and the question on the form is whether you want six more years of that, twelve in all, which is long enough for a parish to become a man's and for a man to stop noticing what he has stopped doing. {@vicar_for_clergy} says, when you call, that most men tick the first box, and that the bishop is grateful when they do, and that the second box is not held against anyone, which is the sentence the diocese uses about things it holds against people. The form is due in three weeks.
events.flavorPrompt: A pastor at the end of his first six years, with a form and three boxes.

choices.label: Tick the first box. Six more years
choices.outcome: The parish is told at the Masses and there is applause at two of them, which embarrasses you and which you will remember. The chancery marks you settled. You are, and the word has a weight the parish does not hear in it: settled men are the last the board thinks of when something opens.

choices.label: Ask for a move instead, and say why in the space provided
choices.outcome: You write two honest sentences about what six years does to a man and a parish. The vicar for clergy calls to make sure you meant it, and you did. The parish will hear in May and some of them will take it personally. The board, which has a use for pastors who will move, writes your name on a different list.

choices.label: Accept, and ask in the same letter for the parochial vicar {parish} was promised
choices.outcome: The chancery does not like conditions, and the vicar for clergy says so, and then says he will see. What you have done is convert six years of goodwill into a request, which is what goodwill is for. Whether a second priest arrives in the house depends on the June list, and the June list depends on things you cannot see.

choices.label: Write that you would take whichever parish the diocese cannot fill, and say so at the deanery
choices.outcome: The offer is unusual enough that the bishop mentions it at the priests' council, without your name, as an example. Two priests guess whose it was. The parish, when it hears you may go, is hurt in the way a parish is hurt by being loved less than the diocese. You have said what you believe obedience is and put your term on the table to prove it.

events.title: Too Useful Where You Are
events.body: {@chancellor} writes to ask whether you would sit on the audit subcommittee of the diocesan finance council, which meets monthly and reads the parish assessments, and which nobody has ever asked to join. A week later {@vicar_general}, over coffee after a funeral, tells you something he perhaps should not: that the bishop had wanted to move you in June, to something better, and that the finance office had talked him out of it, because you are the only priest in the deanery who can read a cash-flow statement and they need one there. He says it as a compliment. It is also a sentence. In {diocese} the men who fix things are kept where the things are, and the men who cannot are moved on to be someone else's problem, and the second kind become pastors of the cathedral. The subcommittee letter is on your desk. It carries the chancellor's signature and, underneath it, in the space where nothing is written, the shape of the next ten years.
events.flavorPrompt: The compliment that is a sentence: the chancery keeping a useful man where he is.

choices.label: Take the subcommittee and do it properly
choices.outcome: You are good at it, which is the problem. Within a year the chancellor sends you the assessments before the meeting for a first read, and the bishop knows your name as the man who catches errors. It is a kind of standing. It is not the kind that gets a man a parish, and everyone on the second floor knows it, and is grateful.

choices.label: Decline, and say in the letter that you were ordained for a parish
choices.outcome: The chancellor is civil about it. The vicar general, who told you the thing over coffee, is briefly cold, because he told you so that you would understand, not so that you would act. The parish gets the Thursday evenings the subcommittee would have taken. The chancery writes nothing down and remembers everything.

choices.label: Take it, and be visibly less useful than they think you are
choices.outcome: It works, slowly. You miss a meeting, you let an error through, you are late with a read. The chancellor stops sending things early. It is the first thing you have done badly on purpose since seminary and you are surprised how easily it comes, and how it feels afterward at Mass.

choices.label: Ask {@bishop} directly whether useful men get parishes in this diocese
choices.outcome: He laughs, which you had not expected, and then answers seriously, which you had not expected either. They do, he says, eventually, and the eventually is the price of being needed. He does not promise anything. He does, at the next board, ask why your name is not on a list, and the finance office has to explain.

events.title: The Joke at the Deanery
events.body: The deanery meets on the second Wednesday in the parish hall of whoever has the best coffee, and this month it is at a parish twenty minutes from {parish} whose pastor, {@brother_priest}, has been there eleven years and has a 10:30 that seats two hundred and draws sixty. Yours draws four hundred and everyone in the room knows the number. He makes the joke during the announcements: something about the fan club, about the traffic on your street on Sundays, about whether the diocese should charge admission. It gets the laugh it was built to get. It is not a cruel joke. It is the joke a man makes when he has been ordained twenty-two years and has watched a younger priest do, apparently without effort, the one thing he has never been able to do, and has decided to be funny about it rather than the alternative. {@vicar_for_clergy} is in the room, because he attends deaneries, and he laughs too, and he is watching your face when you answer, because the joke is not the thing being measured.
events.flavorPrompt: A gifted priest being teased by a brother priest who is not entirely joking.

choices.label: Laugh with the room and let it pass
choices.outcome: You give it the laugh it wanted and the meeting moves on. It was the correct answer and everyone present will forget it by lunch except {@brother_priest}, who will make the joke again in a slightly different form in the spring, because it did not do what he needed it to do.

choices.label: Turn the room to what his parish does that yours cannot, and mean it
choices.outcome: You know what it is, because you have paid attention: the food pantry, the Spanish Mass he built from nothing, the thing he does for the grieving. You say it, plainly, and it is true, and the room hears that it is true. He is disarmed and a little ashamed. The vicar for clergy writes something down that is not about the joke.

choices.label: Say what you think of the joke
choices.outcome: You say it evenly and it takes eight seconds and the room is very quiet afterward. What you said was true. {@brother_priest} goes red and then white, and you have seen, for a moment, the man under the eleven years, and so has everyone else. The deanery will be careful with you now. Careful is not the same as fond.

choices.label: Stop coming to the deanery lunch, and send your apologies each month
choices.outcome: Nobody says anything about it, which is how you know it was noticed. You gain a Wednesday and lose the only room in {diocese} where priests are honest with each other by accident. The joke stops. So does the news. By autumn you hear about a classmate's illness from a parishioner.

events.title: Built Around One Man
events.body: {@vicar_for_clergy} comes for the annual visit and this year he brings a sheet of paper, which he does not usually do. It is the parish you left: the Mass count from the year before you went and the year after, the offertory, the number of young families on the roll. The lines all go the same way. The man who followed you there has said, to his dean, that he inherited a parish built around one priest, and the dean has said it to the second floor, and the second floor has a phrase for it now, which the vicar for clergy uses gently, as if it were a diagnosis: a personal following. He does not say you did anything wrong. He says the board has begun to ask, about you specifically, whether you build parishes or congregations, and that the difference is what they look for when they are choosing a pastor for somewhere that has to outlast him. Then he asks, in the same voice as always, how you are sleeping.
events.flavorPrompt: The chancery has a number for what happened to the parish you left, and a phrase.

choices.label: Say it is true, and say what you would do differently
choices.outcome: He had not expected you to agree, and it changes the visit. You talk for half an hour about what a parish should be able to do without its priest, and he writes most of it down, and some of it appears later in a document the diocese gives new pastors. The board hears that you saw it. That is worth more than not having done it.

choices.label: Say the parish was alive when you left it and the man who followed you let it die
choices.outcome: It may even be true. It is also the one thing a priest cannot say about a brother priest to the vicar for clergy without it going into both files. The deanery hears within a month what you said, and the man you said it about hears it from the deanery, and he has friends. You have kept your record and lost the room.

choices.label: Begin, here, to make {parish} depend on the parish: councils with teeth, lay leaders who can run a Sunday without you
choices.outcome: It is slower and less satisfying than being needed. You hand the RCIA to a catechist who is better than you at it and the funeral lunches to a woman who has always run them anyway. The parish loves you slightly less and works slightly better. In two years the vicar for clergy has a different sheet of paper.

choices.label: Go back for a Sunday and preach for the new man, by name, and tell them to stay
choices.outcome: He agrees to it warily and it is a strange Mass: a church fuller than it has been in a year, for the wrong reason, and you spend the homily telling them the right one. Some of them hear it. The new man is grateful and humiliated in roughly equal measure. The chancery notes that you went, and does not know what to make of it.

events.title: Beloved and Marked
events.body: Two letters come in the same week and it takes you a day to see that they are the same letter. The first is an invitation: a study day for priests, organized by men who think as you do, who have read what you have written and heard what you have preached and would like you to give the paper after lunch, the one people drive in for. They are warm about it. They use the word voice. The second you do not receive; {@closest_classmate} tells you about it. A priest on the other side of the diocese has written to {@vicar_general} to ask, in measured language, whether a man of your known views is the right person to sit on the formation committee, given the range of seminarians the diocese now has. The vicar general has not answered it. He has put it in the file, where it will stay. You have become, without meaning to and by the ordinary means of thinking carefully and saying so, a man one half of the presbyterate is proud of and the other half keeps a folder on.
events.flavorPrompt: A serious theologian discovering he has become a party.

choices.label: Give the paper at the study day, and let it be printed afterward
choices.outcome: The paper is good and the room knows it. It goes into the proceedings and from there to the internet, where it is read by the priest who wrote the second letter, who now has a page number. You have said what you believe with your name on it. The half of the diocese that loves you loves you more. The other half has stopped calling it a folder.

choices.label: Give the paper at the study day, and let it be printed afterward
choices.outcome: The paper is good and the room knows it. It goes into the proceedings and from there to the internet, where it is read by the priest who wrote the second letter, who now has a page number. You have said what you believe with your name on it. The half of the diocese that loves you loves you more. The other half has stopped calling it a folder.

choices.label: Decline the study day, and leave the paper in the drawer
choices.outcome: You write a courteous note about parish commitments and it is accepted with a disappointment you can feel through the envelope. The vicar general, hearing you declined, is quietly relieved. The men who invited you invite someone else, who gives a worse paper, and you sit in the parish with the better one and say nothing.

choices.label: Write to the priest who complained and ask him to lunch
choices.outcome: He is startled and then, to his credit, comes. You disagree for two hours in a diner and neither of you moves an inch and you leave liking each other, which neither of you expected. He does not withdraw the letter. He does, at the next presbyteral council, say you are a serious man, in a tone that ends a conversation someone else had started.

events.title: Very Learned
events.body: {@parishioner} says it at the door after the 9:00, warmly, the way people in {parish} say things they mean as a kindness and a complaint: Father is very learned. You have heard it before. You heard it from the DRE, who wanted the second-grade parents' meeting shorter, and from the Knights, who have stopped asking you to say grace because the grace goes on. The parish is a working parish and it knows what it wants from a priest and it is not, mostly, what you are best at. Then the seminary rector's letter comes: an adjunct post, one course a semester, the bus ride there and back, and a line about the diocese's need for priests who can teach. {@vicar_general}, when you mention it, is pleased in the way he is pleased when a problem has found its own solution. He uses the word future. The word he does not use, but which is in the room, is elsewhere. The letter is a compliment and an exit, and the parish that finds you very learned has not been consulted.
events.flavorPrompt: A scholar in a working parish being gently pulled toward the seminary.

choices.label: Take the adjunct post and keep the parish
choices.outcome: Tuesdays are the seminary and the bus, and the parish learns to do without you on Tuesdays. The students are hungry for what you have and the parish is not, and you feel the difference in your chest each week on the ride back. The chancery has written teacher next to your name in pencil. Pencil becomes ink.

choices.label: Refuse it, and learn to preach for this parish
choices.outcome: It is harder than the seminary would have been. You cut every homily by half and then by half again and lose things that were true and good in the cutting. By Lent the Knights ask you to say grace. The rector writes again the following year and you decline again, and the second refusal is the one the chancery remembers.

choices.label: Teach here instead: a Tuesday night class for anyone in {parish} who comes
choices.outcome: Eleven come the first week and nine the second and the nine stay all year. They are not the parish. They are the part of the parish nobody had noticed was hungry, and they tell people, and the class is fourteen by Easter. The rector's letter goes unanswered. The DRE, who wanted the meetings shorter, joins.

choices.label: Tell {@vicar_general} you would take a university chaplaincy if one came
choices.outcome: He is delighted, and says so, and the delight tells you what the second floor thought of your fit for {parish}. You have named your future and it is not here. The parish does not know yet. The June list, when it comes, will either have your name on it or not, and either way you have stopped pretending.

events.title: Revered
events.body: The parish loves you. That is not a figure of speech; the confessional line is out the door on Saturdays and people who have not been to Mass in years come because of something a neighbor said about the way you say it. The roof over the Lady chapel leaks. It has leaked since Advent and there is a bucket in the third pew that the sacristan moves for funerals. The books are three months behind because the bookkeeper quit in February and you have not read the letter from the diocesan finance office asking why the quarterly report has not come. The finance council chair arrives on a Thursday with the bucket in one hand and the ledger in the other, and sets them both on your desk, and does not sit down. Then {@vicar_general} calls, about something else, and mentions in passing that the bishop has been thinking about parishes that need what he calls a practical man, and you understand that yours is one of them, and that the practical man is not you.
events.flavorPrompt: A holy priest, a bucket, a ledger, and a chancery that has decided he is impractical.

choices.label: Give the chair the books and the roof, and keep the confessional
choices.outcome: He takes them the way a man takes a child he has been waiting to be handed. The roof is fixed in a month at a price you do not ask about and the books are current by the quarter. The chancery hears that the parish is running well and that you are not the one running it, and files both facts.

choices.label: Sit with the new bookkeeper every Thursday until you understand it
choices.outcome: It is dull and it takes the whole spring and you are worse at it than a sixteen-year-old would be. But by summer you can read the quarterly, and you sign the roof contract yourself knowing what it says. The vicar general, told by the chair, stops using the word practical about other people in your hearing.

choices.label: Preach on the widow's mite and ask {parish} for the roof from the pulpit
choices.outcome: They give. Of course they give; they would give you the church if you asked. The roof is paid for in three Sundays and the finance chair is silenced and not persuaded. You have solved the problem with the thing you have instead of the thing you lack, and the chancery, which counts money and not sermons, writes down only the money.

choices.label: Ask the diocese for a loan and a bookkeeper, and admit why
choices.outcome: The finance office sends both, and a letter, and the letter is kind and has the tone of a hospital discharge. The roof is fixed. The books are kept by a woman who reports to the chancellor. You have been honest about what you cannot do and the diocese has taken you at your word, which is what you asked for and not what you wanted.

events.title: The Platform
events.body: The bishop's secretary calls, which he has never done, to say that the editor of the diocesan paper would like a word, and the editor's word is a monthly column, eight hundred words, your name and photograph, on whatever you like. The cathedral rector has asked whether you would preach at the Chrism Mass. A parish across the diocese wants you for its Lenten mission. None of these people have met you. What they have is what you have said, in public, for years, which happens to be what {@bishop} thinks and cannot always say from his own chair. You are being platformed, and everyone in the presbyterate knows the word and knows what it means: that you are going up, quickly, on a rope held by one man. The men who agree with you are glad and the men who do not are counting. The men who are neither, which is most of them, have seen this before and know how it ends, which is with a new bishop and a column that stops without explanation.
events.flavorPrompt: A visible priest being lifted by a bishop who agrees with him; the presbyterate watching.

choices.label: Take the column and write what you believe, monthly, under your name
choices.outcome: The first column is quoted at the priests' council by a man who liked it and by a man who did not. By the sixth you have a readership and a file at the chancery labeled with your name and the word asset. The bishop is pleased. He is sixty-eight. You do the arithmetic and write the seventh column anyway.

choices.label: Take the column and write what you believe, monthly, under your name
choices.outcome: The first column is quoted at the priests' council by a man who liked it and by a man who did not. By the sixth you have a readership and a file at the chancery labeled with your name and the word asset. The bishop is pleased. He is sixty-eight. You do the arithmetic and write the seventh column anyway.

choices.label: Take the column and write only about {parish}: the funerals, the school, the boiler
choices.outcome: It is a good column and nobody quotes it. The editor is puzzled and then, slowly, pleased; readers write in. The bishop's secretary, who had expected something else, says nothing. You have found a way to be seen without being counted, and it will hold exactly until the day someone asks you a direct question in print.

choices.label: Decline all three, with thanks, and stay in the parish
choices.outcome: The secretary is surprised, the editor is offended, and the cathedral rector finds someone else by Friday. Brother priests hear that you turned down the rope and think better of you for it, including some who would have taken it. The bishop, who does not like to be declined, remembers that too.

events.title: The Quiet Burial
events.body: It comes as a letter thanking you for your service on the committee, which you had not resigned from. Then the deanery Chrism Mass rota, which for six years has had you reading, does not. Then {@vicar_for_clergy}, on his visit, mentions the hospital chaplaincy, which is opening, and says with real feeling that it is a real ministry, and looks at you for a beat longer than the sentence needs. Nobody has said anything. Nobody in {diocese} ever does. There is no letter that says the bishop has read what you have said in public for years and has decided that a man who says those things will say them somewhere with fewer people listening. There is only the shape of the thing: the committee, the rota, the chaplaincy, the way the vicar general has started to greet you at clergy days as if you were visiting from another diocese. You are being buried, kindly, in the way a diocese buries a man it cannot answer. The men who agree with you have noticed and gone quiet themselves. That is what it is for.
events.flavorPrompt: A priest opposed to his bishop being moved out of sight by omission rather than decree.

choices.label: Go quiet, and let the record cool
choices.outcome: You stop. Not the belief; the saying. It takes a year for anyone to notice and two for the committee letter to come back, worded as if the first had never been sent. You are, in the chancery's word, rehabilitated. You find you have to work out again what you actually think, having gone so long without saying it.

choices.label: Keep saying it, from the pulpit, in the same voice as before
choices.outcome: The parish hears no difference, because there is none. The chancery hears that there is none. The burial deepens by a committee and a rota and you preach on. Priests who share your views and lost their nerve notice that you have not, and one of them, years later, will say it was the thing that kept him in the diocese.

choices.label: Keep saying it, from the pulpit, in the same voice as before
choices.outcome: The parish hears no difference, because there is none. The chancery hears that there is none. The burial deepens by a committee and a rota and you preach on. Priests who share your views and lost their nerve notice that you have not, and one of them, years later, will say it was the thing that kept him in the diocese.

choices.label: Ask {@vicar_general} to his face what it would take to be trusted again
choices.outcome: He does not pretend not to understand, which you respect. He tells you, in two sentences, and the second sentence is the true one: nothing you can do, and time, and a different bishop. He is not unkind. You leave knowing the size of it, which is better than guessing, and worse than you had let yourself think.

choices.label: Ask for the hospital chaplaincy yourself, before it is offered
choices.outcome: The vicar for clergy is startled and then moved, and the letter comes within the month. It is a real ministry. The dying do not ask what you have said in public and the night shift does not read the diocesan paper. You have taken the burial and made it a choice, and the chancery does not know what to write next to your name.

events.title: The Record
events.body: {@parishioner} brings it to the office in a manila folder, printed out, which is how you know it has been passed around before it reached you. It is a homily you gave years ago in another parish, where it was recorded for the homebound and posted and forgotten, and a letter you wrote to a newspaper the same year. Both say what you believed then, clearly, in your own name. Neither would have caused a ripple where you said them. Here, in {parish}, they have caused something else, and the parishioner is not the only one who has read them; the folder has been to the parish council and, you will learn, to a man on the personnel board who keeps such things. You are not accused of anything. You said what you said, at a volume you chose, and the diocese's memory is longer than the internet's and has better filing. The parishioner asks, reasonably, whether you still think that. Behind the question is the parish, and behind the parish is a folder in the chancery, and both are waiting for the same answer.
events.flavorPrompt: The public record surfacing years later, in a parish or at a board, in a manila folder.

choices.label: Say you meant it then and mean it now
choices.outcome: You say it to the parishioner and, the next Sunday, in slightly different words, to the parish. Some of them leave. More of them, to your surprise, stay, because they had wanted to know whether you were a man who said things or a man who meant them. The board's folder gets a second page, and the second page says consistent, which cuts both ways.

choices.label: Say you have changed your mind since, and say how
choices.outcome: It is true in part and you make it sound true in whole. The parishioner is satisfied. The parish council is satisfied. The man on the board is not, because he has a folder, and the folder now contains the homily, the letter, and the retraction, and men who have all three are described at the chancery with a word that is not consistent.

choices.label: Decline to discuss a homily from another parish and another decade
choices.outcome: You say it politely and it is the correct canonical answer and it satisfies no one. The folder goes on circulating without a reply attached. What the parish concludes is that you have something to be careful about, which is worse than either answer would have been, and which you will spend a year undoing at the door after Mass.

choices.label: Give the printout its context, chapter and verse, and let the parish judge
choices.outcome: You write four pages, footnoted, on what was happening in the Church and the diocese the year you said it and what the words meant in that room. It is the most honest thing you have written and eleven people read it. The eleven include the parish council and the man on the board, who puts it in the folder and, for once, is not sure what to write on the tab.

events.title: A Faction
events.body: They arrive over one winter, without a founding. A lay group in the next county that has a newsletter and has begun quoting you in it. Three priests under forty who drive over for your Sunday Mass and stay for lunch and want to know what you think about things that are not yet questions. A donor, a serious one, who asks what your work needs and means the word work in a way that includes an office and a salary for someone. A dinner in the city at which you are the guest of honor and, you understand halfway through the fish, the point: the people at the table have views and want a man, and you are the man, and they have come to see whether you know it. You have not organized any of this. It has a shape anyway, and a direction, and the chancery has noticed it before you did, because the chancery counts cars in parish lots on Sundays. Something is forming around you that will have your name on it whether or not you give it one.
events.flavorPrompt: A priest who has become a figure realizing that a faction has assembled itself around him.

choices.label: Give it a name and a purpose, and lead it
choices.outcome: It takes a year to become something with letterhead and a second year to be feared. You are now a man the chancery cannot move without a meeting, and the meeting would be about you, and they know it. The presbyterate divides over you in the way it divides over weather. The younger priests are loyal and you are responsible for them now, which is the part nobody warned you about.

choices.label: Point it at the food pantry and the hospital and away from yourself
choices.outcome: The newsletter is bewildered and then, slowly, converted: it starts printing volunteer rotas. The three young priests are put to work and two of them thrive. The donor funds a van. Something still has your name on it, but the name is on a van that delivers groceries, and the chancery, which had a memo drafted, files it instead.

choices.label: Tell them you are a parish priest, and send them home
choices.outcome: The dinner ends early. The newsletter finds a different priest to quote, a worse one. The three young men are hurt and one of them says so, and you find you have no answer he will accept. The chancery breathes out. You are, again, a priest with opinions, and you will know by summer whether that is what you wanted.

choices.label: Take the donor's money for {parish} and nothing else
choices.outcome: You write him a letter with a number in it and a list of what the number buys: the school's boiler, two years of a youth minister, the sacristy roof. He was expecting a movement and receives an invoice. He pays it. The faction does not get its office. The parish gets a boiler. The chancery, which reads gift reports, is unsure whether to be reassured.

events.title: Harder to Bury
events.body: {@vicar_for_clergy} calls to tell you something the diocese does not usually tell a priest, which is what nearly happened to him. The bishop had decided, in April, to move you in June: a parish at the far end of the county, no school, no committee, no reason a man would be sent there except the one everyone would understand. The letter was drafted. Then the petition arrived, four hundred names on it, and the call from the newspaper asking for comment, and two lay members of the finance council who happen to be the bishop's dentist and the diocese's largest donor. The bishop's phone rang for a week. The move is, the vicar for clergy says, postponed, and he says the word carefully, as if it were fragile. You did not organize the petition. You know exactly who did, and so does he. You have become a man the diocese cannot quietly send away, which is a kind of power, and it belongs not to you but to the people who signed, and they will want something for it.
events.flavorPrompt: The chancery tried to move a figure and found it could not; the vicar for clergy tells him so.

choices.label: Let them fight it, and say nothing
choices.outcome: The postponement becomes permanent by the ordinary means of nobody bringing it up. You stay. The parish knows what it did and is proud of it, and its pride has your name in it. The bishop, who was made to look at his own phone for a week, does not forget who he was looking at.

choices.label: Tell them to stop, from the pulpit, and say you will go where you are sent
choices.outcome: It is the hardest homily you have given and the shortest. Some of the four hundred feel betrayed, and say so at the door. The newspaper prints it. The bishop reads it and, for the first time in years, writes to you by hand. The letter for the far parish is not sent. It is not torn up either. It waits, and so do you, and you have said what obedience is with your own future on the table.

choices.label: Go and see {@bishop}, and name your price for going quietly
choices.outcome: He receives you because he must, and you both know it, and it poisons the room before you sit down. You ask for three things and he gives you two, and the giving costs him something in front of his own staff. You will get the parish you wanted. He will get the memory of the afternoon, and he is younger than you.

choices.label: Go anyway, before the letter, and ask for the far parish yourself
choices.outcome: The vicar for clergy is silent for long enough that you check the line. The petition is embarrassed out of existence. The parish is bereft and angry and some of the anger is at you. The far parish gets a priest it did not expect and the bishop gets a problem he cannot name: a man he meant to bury who dug the grave himself and climbed in smiling.

events.title: Twice in March
events.body: {@pastor} says it at breakfast, between the sports page and the second cup, in the voice he uses for things he has decided not to be angry about. {@secretary} tells him you were in the office twice in March. He has the count because she keeps one, in the margin of the appointment book, for every priest who has lived in this house since she came, and he has never asked her to stop. He did the baptism paperwork himself last week, and the bulletin copy the week before, and he is not complaining about the work, which he says he likes, and which is true. He is noticing. He has been a pastor a long time and he knows the difference between a vicar who is out because the parish is out there and a vicar who is out because the office is in here, and he is not sure yet which you are, and he is telling you, over the sports page, that he intends to find out. Then he asks whether you want the last of the eggs.
events.flavorPrompt: A pastor at breakfast, not angry, noticing where his vicar is not.

choices.label: Tell him where you were instead, hour by hour, and let him judge
choices.outcome: You give him the week as it was: the hospital, the school, the two families, the hours in the church. He listens, and at the end he nods once and goes back to the sports page. He has judged. What he concluded he does not say, but the secretary stops keeping the count, and that is his verdict.

choices.label: Take Tuesday mornings in the office, and say so
choices.outcome: You are there at nine on Tuesdays and the phone rings and you answer it and it is, mostly, nothing. The pastor is pleased in the way men are pleased when a point has been taken without an argument. The two families you used to see on Tuesday mornings see you on Thursday afternoons, which is not the same, and one of them stops.

choices.label: Say, pleasantly, that the office is what pastors are for
choices.outcome: It is pleasant and it is also the end of breakfast. He does not answer. He does the bulletin himself again that week, and the week after, and he stops telling you what the secretary counts, which means he has begun to keep the count himself. Priests in the deanery hear you said it and some of them laugh, and it is not entirely with you.

choices.label: Ask {@secretary}, privately, to stop keeping a count
choices.outcome: She is hurt, because the count was never against you; it is how she has kept the house for thirty years. She stops. The pastor notices that she has stopped, and understands why, and it moves the thing from the breakfast table to somewhere he cannot mention it, which is where it will stay and grow.

events.title: Where You Are
events.body: {@parishioner} stops you at the door after the 10:30 and says, without malice, that they never see you. It is a strange thing to say to a priest who has just given them Communion, and it takes you the length of the parking lot to understand what she means. The hospital chaplain knows your car. The night nurses on the fourth floor have your cell number and use it. A family whose mother died in February has told half the parish that you were the only one there at the end, and they are not wrong, and the half of the parish that heard it was moved. The other half has noticed that the office light is off on Wednesday afternoons and that the 10:30 homily was, again, something you thought of in the car. The finance council chair, who is not unkind, says the 10:30 is thin. It is. The fourth floor is not. You are doing the work that made you want to be a priest, and the parish that pays for the car has begun to feel, at the door, like a place you visit.
events.flavorPrompt: A priest who is always at the bedside, and a parish that has begun to notice his absence at the door.

choices.label: Keep the visits. They are the work
choices.outcome: You decide that the fourth floor is the parish too and that the door will have to understand. Some of it does. The families you have sat with are yours for life, and they say so. The 10:30 stays thin. The chancery, which counts the 10:30 and not the fourth floor, writes down what it counts.

choices.label: Cut the visits by half, and be seen at the door and in the office
choices.outcome: The homilies get better because you have Thursdays back. The office light is on. The parishioner who never saw you sees you, and says so, approvingly. The fourth floor gets a chaplain who is not you. A woman dies on a Wednesday night in March and you learn about it on Friday, and it is the first time in years that has happened.

choices.label: Train a team of lay visitors and send them where you cannot be
choices.outcome: Eight people, mostly retired, mostly women, who take the training seriously and the fourth floor more seriously still. Within a year they see more of the sick than you ever did. The parish sees a priest who built something and the hospital sees a parish that shows up. You miss the bedside. It is the right thing and you miss it.

choices.label: Preach, at the 10:30, about where you have been
choices.outcome: It is the best homily you have given in a year because it is the only one you did not think of in the car. You tell them about the fourth floor without names. The parishioner who never saw you is in tears at the door. The finance council chair says nothing, which from him is a great deal. The 10:30 is a little fuller in May.

events.title: The Light at Eleven
events.body: {@brother_priest} drives past the rectory on his way home from a late anointing and sees the light in your window at eleven, and again the next week, and the third time he mentions it at the deanery, lightly, as a question. What are you working on. The question is a kind one and it is also a diocesan question, because in {diocese} a priest's hours are the presbyterate's business and a man who studies three or four evenings a week is either a scholar or hiding, and the deanery would like to know which before it decides how to talk about him. You know what you are working on. You have not told anyone, because it is not finished and because the parish would not understand what it was for, and because there is a pleasure in the hours that you suspect is not entirely holy. The vicar general keeps a list, in his head and probably on paper, of men who could teach. You do not know whether you want to be on it. The brother priest is waiting, with a sandwich, for an answer.
events.flavorPrompt: A brother priest asking, over sandwiches, about the hours a man spends with books.

choices.label: Tell him, and show him the draft
choices.outcome: He reads it in the car in the parking lot and comes back in with a face you have not seen on him before. He asks two questions that are better than any you have asked yourself. It is round the deanery by the next meeting that you are writing something, and the word used is serious, and one of the older men asks for a copy.

choices.label: Say it is nothing, and keep at it
choices.outcome: He accepts it because priests accept such answers from each other. The light stays on. The deanery, denied a story, supplies one, and the one it supplies is that you are a little apart, which is not untrue and is not what you would have chosen to be known for. The work goes on and is better for the silence.

choices.label: Finish it, and send it out under your name
choices.outcome: It is accepted, which surprises you, and printed, which surprises the deanery. The vicar general's list acquires your name in ink. The parish is proud in a way that does not involve reading it. You are now a priest who has published, and that is a sentence the diocese will finish for you, more than once, in ways you did not intend.

choices.label: Move the books to the church, and let the light be taken for prayer
choices.outcome: The window goes dark at ten and the sacristy lamp comes on, and the brother priest, driving past, draws the conclusion you meant him to draw. It is not a lie exactly. You do pray there, some of the time. The work slows, because the sacristy is cold, and you have added to it a small dishonesty that you will notice at Mass for a month.

events.title: From the File
events.body: The letter is addressed to the bishop and forwarded to you by {@vicar_for_clergy} with a note that says only, for your information, which is what he writes on things he wants you to know he has read. A parishioner of {parish}, unnamed, has written to say that the Sunday homilies are read from a book. The parishioner is polite about it. The parishioner is also correct, and you know which book, and which Sundays, and why: the other things you were doing with the hours, the ones nobody at the chancery counts. The vicar for clergy does not ask about the other things. His note does not say the bishop has read the letter, which means the bishop has. What the second floor has in its hand is not a complaint about a homily; it is a data point about a priest who has decided, for reasons of his own, what the parish can do without, and has decided wrong, or at least without asking. You put the letter on the desk next to the book.

choices.label: Write fresh this Sunday, and every Sunday after
choices.outcome: It costs you the hours, and the hours came from somewhere, and something else in the week gets thinner instead. But the 10:30 hears the difference the first week and says so at the door, and the parishioner who wrote does not write again. The vicar for clergy, told by the dean, files the letter under resolved.

choices.label: Write back to {@vicar_for_clergy} with the week as it actually is
choices.outcome: One page: the hours, where they go, what they buy the parish that a homily would not. He reads it and calls, and the call is longer than his calls usually are, and at the end he says that the bishop would like the homilies better anyway. You have been honest and it has been heard and it has changed nothing except that the file now contains your side.

choices.label: Say nothing, and file the letter
choices.outcome: The homilies stay as they are, and so does the week, and the parishioner writes again in the autumn, and this time the note from the vicar for clergy is not for your information. The parish has begun to say among itself that Father is tired, which is kinder than what the chancery says, and less accurate.

choices.label: Admit, to yourself, that the homilies are thin because you are
choices.outcome: You sit with the letter and the book for an hour after the office closes and do not turn on the light. It is not the hours. It is that you have had, for some months, less to say, and the book was where you went so that no one would notice. Nobody at the chancery knows that. You do now, and it is the beginning of something you will have to attend to.

events.title: The Box from the Last Parish
events.body: It comes by parcel post, six weeks after you left, from the parish you left: an album, assembled by the women's guild, with photographs of the farewell lunch and of you at the door of a church that is no longer yours; a check the Knights took up, larger than it should be; a folder of letters from the second grade in pencil. You had the farewell. It was on a Sunday in June and the lunch went on too long and a woman whose husband you buried would not let go of your hand, and you had to be the one to let go, and you did, and drove away, and that was the end of it. Except that it is not. The album is on the desk and the phone has begun to ring with voices you know, asking things the new man there could answer, calling you because they know your number and not his. They are not disloyal to him. They do not know him yet. What you do with the box and the calls will decide, for them and for him, how long it takes.
events.flavorPrompt: Six weeks after a transfer, the old parish arrives in a box.

choices.label: Write to each of them, once, and then stop
choices.outcome: Forty letters over a month, each a page, none of them saying the thing they are for, which is goodbye. You write goodbye anyway, in the last line, in different words each time. The calls thin out by Advent. The album goes on a shelf where you will not see it every day, and you find that is the shelf you look at.

choices.label: Go back for their parish festival in September
choices.outcome: It is a wonderful evening and a mistake. They surround you. The new man stands at the edge of it with a paper plate and a face that has decided to be gracious, and you see it, and it is too late. The chancery hears you went. Brother priests who have been the new man have a word for what you did, and it is not a kind one.

choices.label: Send every call from the old parish to its new pastor, kindly, and mean it
choices.outcome: You say his name to each of them, and his hours, and something true and good about him, and you hang up before they can argue. It is a small discipline and it costs you each time. By spring the calls have stopped. He hears, eventually, what you did, and writes you a note that says only thank you, and you keep it in the album.

choices.label: Give the Knights' check to {parish} for the school, and tell no one where it came from
choices.outcome: The principal is told an anonymous gift has covered the reading specialist for a year, and does not ask. You keep the album and the letters and give away the money, which is the right order. The Knights at the old parish never know. Something of that place is now in this one, in a form only you can see.

events.title: The First Sunday
events.body: The sacristan at {parish} tells you where Father stood. He does not mean it as an instruction. He means it the way a man describes a house he has lived in: this is where the chair was. He also tells you, without your asking, which of the lectors mumbles, which usher counts the collection and which one merely carries it, and that the 8:00 crowd will be counting the minutes of the homily and comparing. They are. You can feel it from the ambo, a congregation weighing a stranger against a memory, and the memory has the advantage of being finished. At the coffee afterward, in a hall that smells of a hundred other coffees, everyone asks the same question in different words: how long are you here for. They have been asked to love a priest before and had him taken, and they would like to know, before they begin, whether it is worth it this time. You cannot tell them. You can only decide what to do with the first month, which is the month they will remember.
events.flavorPrompt: A priest's first Sunday in a new parish: the sacristan, the count, the coffee hour.

choices.label: Do everything the way the last man did, for a year, and change nothing
choices.outcome: You stand where the chair was. The 8:00 counts and is satisfied. The parish relaxes into you the way a body relaxes into a familiar bed, and by Advent they have stopped comparing. The things the last man did wrong you are now doing wrong too, and you have a year to learn which those are before anyone will let you fix them.

choices.label: Change the one thing you cannot preach around, the first week
choices.outcome: You do it on the second Sunday and the 8:00 notices before the first reading. It costs you the coffee hour, which is cold, and three letters, and the sacristan's silence for a month. It also tells the parish who you are, and some of them had wanted to know that more than they wanted the chair left where it was.

choices.label: Spend the first month at kitchen tables, and change nothing yet
choices.outcome: Thirty households in thirty days, coffee and the good cups. You learn who runs the parish, which is not who the council thinks, and what the last man did that nobody will say in the hall. By the time you change anything you know why, and they know you know, and the 8:00 has stopped counting because the count was never the point.

choices.label: Ask the finance council for the books before you ask anyone for anything
choices.outcome: The chair brings them the following Tuesday and watches you read. What is in them explains two things the sacristan said and one he did not. The council decides you are a serious man, and tells the deanery, and the deanery tells the chancery. The parish, which wanted to know how long you were staying, learns instead that you can count, and is not sure what to make of it.

events.title: Father Used To
events.body: The man who had {parish} before you retired to a condominium twenty minutes away and has not, in the parish's sense, left. He is at the 10:30 some Sundays, in the fourth pew on the left, and in the sacristy afterward with the sacristan, and the sacristan is different for the rest of the day. The finance council chair still calls him about the boiler. The bereaved still ask for him for funerals and are told, gently, by the secretary, that Father is retired, and do not believe it, because there he is in the fourth pew. Some of what he did was wrong and you have found the evidence in the files and the walls. All of it was loved. The phrase is everywhere, in the hall and the office and at the door: Father used to. It is not said against you. It is said the way people say the names of the dead, except that he is not dead, and is in the parking lot after the 10:30 talking to the ushers about the collection, which is no longer his.
events.flavorPrompt: The retired predecessor, twenty minutes away and in the fourth pew.

choices.label: Ask him to concelebrate at Christmas, and say from the pulpit that he is always welcome
choices.outcome: He is moved, and the parish is moved, and the fourth pew becomes a kind of honor rather than a reproach. He begins to come less, oddly, once he is asked to come. The finance chair still calls him about the boiler, but the boiler is fixed now, and eventually there is nothing to call about.

choices.label: Ask him, privately, to stay away for a year
choices.outcome: He takes it badly, because it is a hard thing to be asked, and because he had not understood that he was doing anything. He stays away. The parish notices and draws its own conclusions, and the conclusions are not all in your favor. But the sacristy is yours by Lent, and the finance chair, denied his phone call, learns to bring the boiler to you.

choices.label: Ask {@vicar_for_clergy} to have the word with him, so that you need not
choices.outcome: The word is had, and it works, and the fourth pew is empty from the following Sunday. The retired man knows who asked. So, within the month, does every retired priest in the diocese, who have a network and long memories. You have solved a problem by handing it upward, and the chancery keeps a list of men who do that.

choices.label: Go to the condominium with a bottle and ask him what he wishes he had done
choices.outcome: He talks for three hours and most of it is worth having: which families to watch, which donor to never take money from, where the water comes in. Toward the end he tells you the thing he did wrong, unasked, and it is the thing you found in the files, and it costs him to say it. You leave with a friend and a map.

events.title: What Happened After You Left
events.body: {@closest_classmate} calls on a Sunday evening, which is when priests call each other with things that cannot wait until the deanery, and tells you about the parish you left. The choir is gone; its director followed you out the door, in spirit if not in fact, and quit in the autumn. The young adults do not meet. The collections are down by a third and the finance council has written to the chancery. The new man is a good priest, your classmate says, carefully, and he is drowning, and the thing he is drowning in is you: the parish talks about you at the door, at the council, in the confessional, and it is not helping him, and he has begun, without meaning to, to hate a man he has never met. Your classmate is not blaming you. He is telling you because someone should, and because the diocese is a small place and the story is being told in it, with your name, in a tone you would not choose. You had a parish that loved you. This is what that turned out to cost, and it is not you who is paying.

choices.label: Go back for one Sunday, and preach for him, not for them
choices.outcome: He agrees warily. The church is full for the wrong reason and you use the homily to give them the right one, by name, his name, three times. Some of them hear it. He shakes your hand in the sacristy afterward with the face of a man who has been helped and would rather not have needed it. The choir director comes back in Advent.

choices.label: Write to the new pastor: everything you know about the place, and nothing about yourself
choices.outcome: Six pages: the families, the donor to avoid, the usher who runs the parish, where the water comes in. Not a word of advice and not a word of apology. He does not answer for two months and then answers with a page that says he used all of it. Your classmate says the story in the diocese has changed its tone, slightly.

choices.label: Say nothing. It is his parish
choices.outcome: It is the correct answer and it is also, your classmate says before he hangs up, the easy one. You sit with that. The parish you left goes on shrinking for a year and then, slowly, without you, stops. The new man survives it. He never writes. You are not sure you would have either.

choices.label: Tell {@vicar_for_clergy} the man was the wrong appointment for that parish
choices.outcome: You say it in the language of concern and he hears it in the language it was in. It goes in a file, and the file is not the new man's. The deanery hears within a month what you said about a brother priest who inherited your parish, and the brother priests, who have all been the new man somewhere, close a door you did not know was open.

events.title: Before He Signs It
events.body: The personnel office sends the form every spring: the pastor's evaluation of his parochial vicar, four pages, boxes and lines, to be returned by the end of May and never shown to the vicar. {@pastor} does something pastors do not do. He puts it on the breakfast table, filled in, unsigned, and says you can read it if you want, and that he will sign it either way. Then he takes his coffee to the porch. It is his handwriting, which is small and does not waste ink. Some of it you knew. Some of it you had not known he had noticed, and the noticing is the surprise: the hours you thought were private, the thing you did for the family in March that you told no one. There is one line that is unfair and it is the only line he has underlined. What he has written says as much about him as about you, and he knows that, and has left it on the table anyway, and is on the porch waiting to find out what kind of man reads it and what kind does not.
events.flavorPrompt: A pastor leaves his evaluation of his vicar on the breakfast table, unsigned.

choices.label: Read it, thank him, and let it go to the chancery as written
choices.outcome: You take it to the porch and say thank you and mean it, including for the underlined line, which you will think about. He signs it at the railing. It goes in the file, and the file is the better for it. You know now what he sees and, from what he chose to see, what he is, which was the more valuable of the two.

choices.label: Argue the underlined line, on the porch, before he signs
choices.outcome: He listens. He does not change it. He says why, and the why is the first fully honest thing he has said to you about yourself, and it goes in nowhere but the porch. You have seen what he is when contradicted, which is the thing the form cannot tell the chancery and that you will need to know for the rest of the year.

choices.label: Leave it on the table unread. It is his to write
choices.outcome: He comes in from the porch and finds it where he left it and looks at you for a moment, and signs it standing up. He does not say anything. You will never know what the file says, and he knows that you chose that, and it is a kind of trust, and he treats you, from then on, as a man who can be trusted with things.

choices.label: Ask him to write the harder version, the one that would actually help you
choices.outcome: He is quiet, and then he takes the form back and rewrites two pages of it at the kitchen table while you wait. The new version is not kind and it is exact, and the chancery, which reads a hundred of these, reads this one twice. You learn more about yourself in an hour than in the year before it, and more about him than he meant to tell you.

events.title: Not Ready, and Please Keep Him
events.body: {@brother_priest} tells you at the deanery, because he thinks you should know, what {@pastor} said about you at the deans' meeting, where pastors are asked once a year about the men in their houses. He said you were not ready. He also said, in the same breath, that he would very much like to keep you another year, and the deans, who have heard the two sentences together before, wrote down the second one. It is not what he says at breakfast. At breakfast he says you are the best vicar he has had, and that is probably also true, and the two things are one thing: a pastor who has found a man who makes his parish work does not, if he is honest with himself, want that man made a pastor in June, and the way you keep such a man is to say he is not ready in the one room where it counts. He is not lying about you. He is protecting himself with the truth, chosen carefully. You are the thing being kept.
events.flavorPrompt: A vicar learning that his pastor's praise and his pastor's veto are the same sentence.

choices.label: Ask him at breakfast whether he said it
choices.outcome: He does not deny it, which you had not expected, and then he explains it, which you had, and the explanation is the one you had already worked out. It sits between you for a week. Then it does not. You know now that he will keep you if he can, and that he knows you know, and the house is a little colder and a little more honest.

choices.label: Take the compliment inside the sentence, and stay
choices.outcome: You decide that a parish that works and a pastor who wants you is not the worst place to spend a year that would otherwise be spent waiting. He never knows you heard. The parish gets your best year. The June list, when it comes, does not have your name on it, and you find you had already made your peace with that in April.

choices.label: Tell {@vicar_for_clergy} you are ready, and let the file hold both opinions
choices.outcome: He listens with the expression of a man who has heard a vicar and a pastor disagree about the vicar before, which he has, many times. He writes it down.
