The file now says two things and the board will decide which it believes. The pastor learns you went, because pastors learn such things, and the breakfasts are shorter.

choices.label: Ask {@brother_priest} to say to the dean, at the next meeting, what he thinks of you
choices.outcome: He does, because he offered before you asked. The dean hears a second pastor's view of a vicar, which is unusual, and passes it upward with a note. It is a small thing and a favor and you owe it now. The pastor, hearing that another priest spoke for his vicar, is not sure whether to be pleased or robbed.

events.title: The Other Form
events.body: The personnel office has a new form this year, and it comes to you and not to {@pastor}: a confidential assessment of the parish and its leadership, to be completed by the parochial vicar and returned in the enclosed envelope, which is addressed to {@vicar_for_clergy} personally. The covering letter explains that the diocese wishes to hear from the men who live in its rectories as well as the men who run them. It has boxes. One of the boxes is about the pastor's stewardship of the parish's finances. One is about his availability to the people. One, at the bottom, is a blank space labeled other observations, and it is the one the vicar for clergy will read first. You know what you would write if it were true that no one would see it. You also know that {@pastor} will learn the form exists, because pastors do, and that the deanery will know within a year which vicars filled it in, and how, because the deanery always knows. You have a week, an envelope, and a pastor across the breakfast table who has not yet been told.
events.flavorPrompt: A confidential form asking the vicar to grade his pastor; the envelope and the breakfast table.

choices.label: Fill it in truthfully, every box, and the blank space too
choices.outcome: It takes an evening and you do not enjoy it. The vicar for clergy calls afterward to thank you, which he does not do for the men who wrote nothing. The pastor never sees it. He guesses, from the vicar for clergy's manner at the next clergy day, that something was said, and looks at you across the breakfast table with a question he does not ask.

choices.label: Write the version he would sign himself
choices.outcome: Satisfactory in every box and a paragraph in the blank space about the parish's strengths. It is not untrue. It is also not what the form was for, and the vicar for clergy, who has read forty of these, knows exactly what a page of satisfactory means and files it accordingly. The breakfasts stay warm. The file learns nothing.

choices.label: Return it blank, with a note that vicars should not be asked to grade pastors
choices.outcome: The note is two sentences and it is repeated at the priests' council by a pastor who was delighted by it. The vicar for clergy is not delighted. The brother priests, who have all been vicars, think better of you, and some of them say so. The chancery has learned you have views on how it does its business, and files that in the box marked other observations.

choices.label: Fill it in truthfully, and show it to him before you send it
choices.outcome: He reads it at the kitchen table in silence and then says one thing about the finances box that changes what you had written, and you change it, because he was right. The rest he leaves. It goes to the chancery with both of you knowing what it says, which no other form in the diocese can claim. You have seen him read himself, which told you the rest.

events.title: What Should I Tell Them
events.body: The personnel board has written to {@pastor} to ask, in the form of words it uses, whether in his judgment his parochial vicar is ready to be entrusted with a parish of his own. It is the question that matters and he knows it, and he does the thing that is either the greatest compliment he has paid you or a way of not having to decide: he brings the letter to the study after dinner, sits down, and asks you what he should tell them. He is serious. He has been asked this about other men and answered without consulting them. He is consulting you, and whatever you say he will weigh, and whatever he writes will go into a room where the June list is made and will be read by men who will not know it was partly your sentence. It is an honest question and there is no honest answer that is not also a claim about yourself, made to the man who has watched you for years, who will know if you are wrong.
events.flavorPrompt: A pastor asking his vicar what to tell the board about the vicar.

choices.label: Tell him you are ready, and why, in three sentences
choices.outcome: You have the three sentences because you have thought about them for a year. He listens, and nods, and writes something that night which he does not show you. It was, you learn later, mostly your sentences with one of his own added, and the one of his own was the one the board quoted.

choices.label: Tell him to write what he sees
choices.outcome: He is quiet for a moment and then says that is what he had hoped you would say. What he writes you never learn. The board makes its list and you are on it or you are not, and either way it was his sentence and not yours, which is what the form asked for and, you decide, what you would have wanted anyway.

choices.label: Tell him you are not ready, and mean it
choices.outcome: He looks at you for a long time and then says that it is the first time a vicar has told him that, and that he does not agree, and that he will write what he thinks. Whether the board hears your no or his yes you do not know. What you know is that you said the true thing in the one room where it cost you, and he saw you say it.

choices.label: Ask him what the board weighs, and give him the evidence for each thing
choices.outcome: He tells you: results, temperament, money, the people. You give him a page, with numbers, for each. He reads it and says, not warmly, that it is very thorough. He writes to the board that night. Whatever he wrote, it was informed, and the board remarks on that, and the remark, when it reaches him, is not entirely a compliment to either of you.

events.title: Use Your Judgment
events.body: The title says you are keeping the seat warm. Parochial administrator: the powers of a pastor, the canon says, without the stability, and everyone in {parish} has looked the phrase up and understood the second half. The school principal needs the teachers' contracts for next year signed by Friday, all eleven of them, and the finance council chair has said, in a meeting, that a decision of that size should wait for the pastor, when there is one, and looked at you when he said it. The principal has said that if the contracts are not signed by Friday she will lose two teachers to the public system and the fourth grade will have thirty-four children in it. {@vicar_general}, when you call, says to use your judgment. That is the sentence the chancery uses before it judges a man's judgment. Whatever you sign or do not sign will be read in June as evidence, by the same people who have not yet decided whether the seat is yours, and the principal is in the outer office with the folder.
events.flavorPrompt: An administrator asked to make a pastor's decision without a pastor's title.

choices.label: Sign the contracts, all eleven, as the pastor would
choices.outcome: You sign them on Thursday and the principal cries in the outer office, briefly, from relief. The finance chair says nothing at the next meeting, which is a concession. The chancery learns that you decided, and how quickly. In June that will be read as either decisiveness or presumption, depending on who is reading and what else is in the file.

choices.label: Send the folder to the chancery for a signature
choices.outcome: It comes back signed in nine days by the vicar general, with a note, and the note is polite and one line and says that in future such matters are within the administrator's competence. Two teachers have gone. The fourth grade has thirty-four children. You have been careful and it has been noticed, and careful is not a word the board uses about men it makes pastors.

choices.label: Renew ten, decline one, and explain the one to the principal and the council
choices.outcome: The one is the position the budget could not carry and everyone knew it and no pastor had been willing to say so. You say so. The principal is furious and then, a month later, grateful. The finance chair, who had wanted you to wait, finds he has been given what he actually wanted. The chancery reads a decision with a reason attached, which is rarer than it should be.

choices.label: Call the last pastor and ask what he would do
choices.outcome: He tells you, from his retirement, in detail, and you do most of it. It is good advice and it is his, and the parish, which loved him, hears that you asked and likes you for it. The chancery hears too and is less sure: an administrator who calls the last man is either humble or not yet a pastor, and the board has not decided which.

events.title: The Test You Cannot See
events.body: {@vicar_general} calls on the first Monday of every month, which he does not do for pastors, and asks how things are, and listens, and does not say what he does with the answer. The finance council chair, you have learned from the secretary, has a friend at the chancery and a monthly lunch. Parishioners ask at the door whether you are staying, and the honest answer is that no one has told you, and you have stopped giving the honest answer because it frightens them. You are being tested and nobody will say what the test is or when it ends or what a passing mark looks like. What you know is that the diocesan appeal is in March, and that the parish's number will be on a sheet the bishop sees before he sees anything else about {parish}, and that the number is the one thing about your year that will fit in a column. It is not the most important thing you will do here. It is the thing that will be counted.
events.flavorPrompt: An administrator watched from the chancery through a monthly phone call and a finance chair's lunches.

choices.label: Run the appeal hard. The number is the grade
choices.outcome: You preach it three Sundays running and phone the top forty givers yourself, and the parish makes its goal for the first time in six years. The bishop sees the number. He does not see the two families who stopped coming because they were phoned. The vicar general's Monday call is shorter in April, and warmer.

choices.label: Run the parish as if no one were watching
choices.outcome: The appeal is announced once and reaches what it reaches, which is short. The Monday calls continue. What the vicar general hears, month after month, is a man doing the work without performing it, and it is either exactly what the board wants or exactly what it cannot measure. You will find out in June. The parish, meanwhile, has a priest.

choices.label: Ask him, on the Monday call, what the bishop is actually looking for
choices.outcome: There is a pause, and then he tells you, because you asked directly and because he likes you, and it is not the appeal. It is something about the school and something about the last pastor's debts and you would not have guessed either. The call ends. You now know the test, which is more than any administrator in the diocese has known, and the knowing is its own kind of burden.

choices.label: Have the finance chair to dinner and tell him you know who he has lunch with
choices.outcome: He goes red and then, to his credit, laughs, and the dinner is better after that. The lunches continue. What changes is what he says at them, because he has been seen, and men who have been seen report differently. You have made an ally of a spy by refusing to pretend he was anything else, and the chancery's picture of you acquires a second source.

events.title: If It Were Offered
events.body: {@bishop} comes for confirmation, sixty candidates and a warm church, and does it well, and afterward in the car park, while his secretary is finding the keys, he asks you the question the diocese does not ask administrators: whether you would want {parish}, if it were offered. He says if. He is a careful man and the if is real; the board has not met and the terna, if there is one, has not been drawn. But he is asking, and the asking is the nearest thing to the room you will ever be let into, and he is looking at you over the roof of the car with the expression of a man who has to fill a parish and would like, for once, to know what the priest thinks before he decides. You know what {parish} needs. You have run it for a year. You know whether you are that man or whether you have merely kept it warm for him, and the secretary has found the keys.
events.flavorPrompt: The bishop in the car park after confirmation, asking the administrator if he would want the parish.

choices.label: Say yes, and say what you would do with it in the time it takes him to open the door
choices.outcome: You have it ready: three things, in order. He listens with the door open and then closes it again and asks a question about the second one. The secretary waits. When he goes, he says he will remember, and he is a man who does. The board will meet without you in it, but it will meet with a sentence of yours in the bishop's mouth.

choices.label: Say the parish needs a different man, and name what kind
choices.outcome: He is very still, and then he asks you to say it again, and you do, and he thanks you in a voice you have not heard him use. You have told a bishop the truth against your own interest in a car park and he has heard it. Whether he acts on it you learn in June. What you learned tonight is what he is like when told something he did not expect, and it was worth the parish.

choices.label: Say yes, if the school's debt is restructured and a vicar comes with it
choices.outcome: He raises his eyebrows, which on him is an event. Then he asks what the debt is, and you tell him to the dollar, and he says he had not been told that number. The conversation goes on past the secretary's patience. You have negotiated with a bishop over a car roof, and he has let you, and the board will hear that the administrator knows what the parish costs.

choices.label: Say you will go where you are sent
choices.outcome: He nods, because it is the right answer and he has heard it a thousand times, and gets into the car. It was true and it was also a way of not answering, and he knows both. The board will meet without a sentence from you. What it has instead is a year of the parish's numbers, and a bishop who was told nothing in a car park and remembers that too.

events.title: The Bearing
events.body: {@vicar_for_clergy} says it at the end of the annual visit, standing, with his coat on: that you have the bearing. He does not explain. He does not need to; you have been in rooms before this one and you know what it means when a man with a legal pad says a thing like that on his way out. It means the board has been talking, three years in, about a parish. {@rival_classmate}, ordained at twenty-six, has been a vicar for nine years and is a vicar still. He says it at the clergy day, in the lunch line, to no one in particular and loud enough: they are giving the parishes to the old guys. It is not untrue. The diocese reads a man who came to the seminary with a mortgage and a career behind him as someone who will not have to be taught what a budget is or how to speak to a finance chair his own age, and it is right, mostly, and the men who were ordained young and have waited a decade are watching you be right, and you have to stand in the lunch line with them.
events.flavorPrompt: A late vocation being promoted for his bearing, in a lunch line full of men who waited longer.

choices.label: Let them think it. It is true enough
choices.outcome: You do not answer the lunch line and you do not decline the vicar for clergy's sentence. The parish, when it comes, comes. Some of the younger men are friends and remain friends and some are not and do not. You have taken the advantage you were given and it is the diocese's to give, and you tell yourself that on the days it is hard to.

choices.label: Tell {@vicar_for_clergy} the younger men have waited longer, and say a name
choices.outcome: He writes the name down, which you had not expected, and says it is generous, which he had not expected to say. Whether it changes the June list you never know. It changes the lunch line, because the man whose name you said hears that you said it, and it changes something in you that had been getting comfortable.

choices.label: Take {@rival_classmate} to lunch and let him say it to your face
choices.outcome: He says it, at length, and it is worse than the lunch line and more honest, and at the end of it he is tired and so are you. You do not agree and you do not have to. He has been heard by the man he resents, and it is not nothing, and the next clergy day he says the thing again, but quieter, and not while you are in the line.

choices.label: Say plainly, to the line, that you ran things before, and that it counts
choices.outcome: It is true and it silences the line, which is not the same as persuading it. The men who heard it will repeat it, and the version they repeat has less of the plainness and more of the edge. The chancery, hearing the repeated version, is not displeased: it confirms what the board thought about bearing. The younger men have a new thing to say about you, and it is that you said that.

events.title: Pastor at Thirty-One
events.body: The finance council chair is your father's age and has told you so, twice, once as a kindness and once as something else. The DRE resigned on Tuesday, in writing, citing direction, and the school principal has asked for a meeting about the principal's contract, which you have not read. You have not had a day off since Advent. The bishop, {@vicar_for_clergy} said when the letter came, had every confidence, and you believed him, and you were the youngest pastor in {diocese} by six years and the parish said so at the reception with pride, and the pride has lasted about as long as the casseroles. It is not that you cannot do the work. It is that there is no one in the house to ask and no one at the deanery who was your age when they did this, and the men who were vicars for twelve years and resented you for it are watching now with a patience that is worse than gloating. The chair has asked for the budget by Friday. You are, in the word priests use about each other and never about themselves, underwater.

choices.label: Call {@vicar_for_clergy} and say the word
choices.outcome: He is silent and then he is kind, and the kindness is practical: a retired pastor to sit with you on Thursdays for the spring, a bookkeeper on loan, a sentence to the bishop that he chooses carefully. It goes in the file. The file now says that at thirty-one you asked for help, and in ten years that will read as either weakness or wisdom, depending on what you did with it.

choices.label: Ask {@brother_priest}, who has done this for twenty years, to walk you through one year of it
choices.outcome: He says yes before you finish asking, because nobody asked him, ever, and he has been waiting to be asked. Lunch every other Wednesday and a phone call whenever. He teaches you the budget in a month and the finance chair in two. The deanery notices that you asked one of them, and it changes what the patient men are waiting for.

choices.label: Keep going. Sleep in the summer
choices.outcome: You do the budget by Friday and it is adequate and the chair says so, in that tone. You hire a DRE. You read the principal's contract at two in the morning. By Easter you have not preached a homily you would want to hear and by Pentecost you have stopped noticing. The parish runs. Something in you does not, and it will be a while before anyone, including you, looks for it.

choices.label: Give the chair the budget, the DRE's assistant the DRE's job, and keep the altar
choices.outcome: The chair is startled to be handed what he has been demanding, and does it well, and is yours from then on. The assistant is better than the DRE was. You keep the Masses and the confessional and the door, which is what you were ordained for, and the parish notices a priest who is present. The chancery notices a pastor who does not do his own budget, and is of two minds.

events.title: Time on Your Side
events.body: The bishop's secretary takes you aside after the Chrism Mass and asks whether you have thought about further studies. He says it as if the thought were yours. Rome, or Washington; canon law or theology, whichever you lean toward; two years, perhaps three, and the diocese would pay. The bishop, he says, invests in men who have time, and you have time: ordained under thirty, a whole career in front of you, no hurry. What he does not say, and what you can hear under the sentence, is that no hurry means no parish, not for years; that the men ordained at thirty-eight are pastors at forty-one and you are meant to be in a library at thirty-two, being formed for something the bishop has in mind and will not name. It is a compliment. It is also a decision about your next decade made by a man who has never seen you say Mass, on the basis of your birth certificate. The secretary is waiting, pleasantly, with the bishop's car idling behind him.
events.flavorPrompt: A young priest being groomed for graduate study while the late vocations get parishes.

choices.label: Say yes to the studies: theology, and the years it takes
choices.outcome: The secretary is pleased and the bishop, at the next clergy day, mentions you by name as an example of the diocese's future, which the men ordained at thirty-eight hear with a particular expression. You will be gone for years. The parish will get someone else. What you come back as is not decided yet, and neither is who will be bishop when you do.

choices.label: Ask for canon law, which is the road to the chancery, and say so
choices.outcome: The secretary's eyebrows go up, because men do not usually name the road, and then he smiles, because the bishop likes men who know where they are going. The chancellor hears within the week and takes you to lunch. You have said out loud what the grooming is for, and the diocese, which prefers such things unsaid, has decided to find it refreshing.

choices.label: Say you want a parish, and would rather wait ten years for one than leave for a degree
choices.outcome: The secretary is surprised and then, briefly, something else: a man who was himself sent to Rome at thirty and has been carrying a bishop's briefcase ever since. He says he will pass it on. He does. The bishop is puzzled by a young man who does not want what he is offered, and puzzled men are not always generous, and you will wait, and the parish will be worth it or it will not.

choices.label: Ask him what the studies are for, in the bishop's mind
choices.outcome: He is not supposed to say and he half does, because the question was a fair one and he was young once. It is a job, eventually, and the job has a title, and the title is not pastor. You have learned what the diocese thinks you are for, which most men learn at fifty. Whether you want to be that is now a question you can ask on purpose.

events.title: The Year of the Letters
events.body: Six pastors turn seventy-five in the same twelve months, and this year the bishop, who has refused such letters for a decade, accepts four of them, because two of the four have written twice and one has written from a hospital bed. The June list is the longest anyone in {diocese} remembers, and it is not long enough. {@vicar_for_clergy} calls every priest under sixty, in alphabetical order, and when he reaches you he does not pretend it is a courtesy call. He asks whether you could take a second parish for a while, the one eleven miles from {parish} whose pastor has just retired to his sister's house in Florida. Two Sunday schedules. Two finance councils. A rectory nobody will live in. He says the bishop will be grateful, and that gratitude in a year like this is the currency the diocese has, and that men who help in the year of the letters are remembered in the years after. He is not wrong. He is also asking you to do two men's work, and he knows what that costs, because he did it once, and his voice says so.
events.flavorPrompt: A retirement wave: the vicar for clergy calling every priest under sixty, alphabetically.

choices.label: Take the second parish
choices.outcome: It is what everyone says it is. You learn a second sacristy in the dark and a second finance chair's temper and where the second boiler is. The bishop writes by hand. In two years, when the chancery is choosing men for things, your name is on a short list that is called, informally, the ones who helped. Your own parish sees less of you and forgives it, mostly.

choices.label: Say your own parish is all you can carry, and mean it
choices.outcome: He says he understands, and he does, and he writes it down anyway, because everything is written down in the year of the letters. Your parish gets the whole of you. The second parish gets a retired priest from another diocese who says Mass and nothing else. The list called the ones who helped does not have your name on it, and you will hear the list mentioned for a decade.

choices.label: Offer to cover the Masses there, not the parish
choices.outcome: He takes it, because half a priest is what he can get. You say the 7:30 there and the 9:00 and 11:00 here and are in the car between them every Sunday for a year. The parish eleven miles away is grateful for the Masses and gets no one for the rest, and the finance council there writes to the chancery, and the letter does not mention you, which is the best that could be hoped.

choices.label: Give {@vicar_for_clergy} the names of three men who could, and why each
choices.outcome: He had two of the three on his own list and had not thought of the third, and the third is the one who takes it. You have helped in the year of the letters without taking the parish, and the chancery, which knows the difference, values it differently: less than the men who took parishes and more than the men who said no. The third man never learns who said his name.

events.title: For Want of a Priest
events.body: The parish twenty minutes from {parish} is closing. Not merging, the decree is careful to say, and not for money, though the money is not good; it is closing because there is no priest for it and will not be one, and the bishop has decided that a church with a Mass once a month said by a man driving from somewhere else is not a parish. Its people are to be, in the decree's word, welcomed at {parish}. The decree has been read to them by the vicar general at a Sunday Mass and they did not take it well, and there is a petition, and a letter from a lawyer that will go nowhere. {@vicar_for_clergy} asks whether you will say the last Mass there, on the feast of the parish's patron, because the bishop cannot and the vicar general should not, and because it should be the priest who will have them afterward. Their finance council has eighty thousand dollars in a building fund for a building that will be sold. Whether it comes with the people or goes to the diocese is a question the decree does not answer, and the people have noticed.
events.flavorPrompt: A parish closing for want of a priest; the last Mass, and the people who will be welcomed.

choices.label: Say the last Mass, and preach the truth about why it is the last
choices.outcome: You tell them it is not their fault and not the money and that the diocese does not have enough priests and that this is what that means, in a building, on a feast day. Some of them weep. The vicar general, at the back, does not move. The newspaper prints a paragraph. The chancery reads the paragraph and understands that you told the truth and did not tell it against anyone, and is not sure that is better.

choices.label: Say the Mass, and then build the welcome: their statues in your church, their choir in yours, their names in the bulletin
choices.outcome: It takes a year and it is the best thing you do that year. Their Saint Anthony stands in your side aisle and their choir sings the 9:00 and their names are in the bulletin under a heading you invented. Some of them come and some of them go to the parish in the next diocese out of spite, and the building fund comes with the ones who came, because you asked.

choices.label: Refuse to say the Mass, and say the bishop should close what he closes
choices.outcome: The vicar for clergy is silent on the phone and then says he will tell the bishop, and does. The bishop says the Mass himself, which was, you think, the point, and preaches well, and does not look at you at the deanery for a year. The brother priests, who have all been asked to do the diocese's hard thing for it, are quietly with you. The closed parish's people come to {parish} anyway, unsure what you did.

choices.label: Ask the bishop, in a letter with your name on it, for a year to find them a priest
choices.outcome: The letter is leaked within the week, not by you, and the paper prints it, and for a month you are the priest who fought the closing. The bishop gives the year, because he had no choice, and no priest is found, because there is none, and the last Mass is said a year later by you, to people who now believe you tried. The chancery has a new page for you, and it is not the one about bearing.
